The $40 Mistake That Cost One Breeder Three Thousand Bucks

Disclosure: PawCritic is reader-supported. A few links below are Amazon affiliate links, and we may earn a small commission if you purchase through them at no extra cost to you.

I once watched a friend lose nearly his entire ball python collection to a snake he'd owned for exactly nine days. He skipped quarantine because the new animal 'looked healthy' and came from a breeder with a good reputation. Within six weeks, three females were dead from a viral infection the newcomer had been quietly carrying, and two more ended up at the vet with breathing problems that took months of antiviral care and antibiotics to sort out. He spent around $3,000 in vet bills. A quarantine tub, a spare thermostat, and 60 days of patience would have cost him about $150.

That's the whole argument for quarantine in a nutshell. Reptiles are masters at hiding illness. It's what they do — a lizard that looks sick in the wild gets eaten, so millions of years of evolution have built animals that can be genuinely dying while displaying nothing more obvious than 'sitting still a lot.' When you bring a new animal home, you cannot see what it's carrying. Not mites, not hookworms, not cryptosporidia, not a developing respiratory infection. Only time and testing reveal those, and quarantine is how you buy that time without betting your existing animals on the outcome.

Yet in my experience, fewer than half of hobbyists quarantine at all, and most of the ones who do cut the duration short or house the new animal in the same room with open-topped tubs stacked next to their collection. So here's the protocol I've used and refined over roughly two decades of keeping, breeding, and occasionally learning things the expensive way.

What Quarantine Actually Means (and What It Doesn't)

Quarantine isn't just 'keeping the new animal in a different cage.' A proper quarantine is physical separation in a separate room, on separate equipment, handled in a specific order, for a minimum of 60 days — 90 for snakes, and longer if anything suspicious shows up. Some keepers in the biosecurity-obsessed corners of the hobby go six months for high-risk animals like wild-caught imports or snakes from large mixed collections. That's not paranoia; ranavirus, nidovirus, cryptosporidiosis, and inclusion body disease can all sit dormant or low-grade for extended stretches.

The three pillars are simple. Separation: a different room entirely, ideally one with a door. Dedicated equipment: your quarantine tub gets its own tongs, water bowl, spray bottle, hooks, and paper towels, and nothing from that room travels to your main collection without disinfection. Order of operations: you always handle, feed, and clean your established animals FIRST and the quarantined animal LAST, and you wash up in between. If you do those three things consistently, you've eliminated the vast majority of transmission risk.

What quarantine doesn't mean is a bare tub with no heat because 'it's just temporary.' A cold, stressed reptile is an immunocompromised reptile, and stress alone can let a dormant pathogen flare into a detectable one. You need the quarantine setup to hit proper temperatures. That's non-negotiable, and it's the single most common way people sabotage their own quarantine.

Building the Quarantine Setup: Simple, Cheap, and Deliberately Sterile

You want the opposite of a fancy naturalistic vivarium. Paper substrate, minimal decor, one or two simple hides, a water bowl you can scrub or toss. The goal is an enclosure you can fully disinfect, because you'll be cleaning it frequently and you want to see everything — every stool, every mite, every speck of anything — against white paper towels or unprinted newsprint.

A plastic tub or a basic glass tank in the 20-to-40-gallon range works for most lizards and smaller snakes. The setup I keep on standby at all times is a 32-quart plastic tub with a thermostat-controlled heat mat under one third, a strip of thermostatic heat rope as backup, a digital thermometer with a probe on the hot end, two cardboard or resin hides, and a heavy ceramic water dish. Total cost if you're buying fresh: somewhere around $80-120. That's it. I've used that same tub for dozens of animals over the years.

Temperature control is where I see people cut corners, and it drives me nuts. A thermostat isn't optional equipment for a heat mat — unregulated heat mats can exceed 120 degrees Fahrenheit and will burn a snake that has nowhere thermally appropriate to go in a bare tub. I use a reliable proportional thermostat like the Herpstat-style thermostat on every quarantine setup I've ever run, and I consider it the one component worth spending real money on. Pair it with a cheap digital probe thermometer placed directly on the tub floor over the mat, because air temperature readings tell you almost nothing about the surface a belly-sitting animal is actually touching. You want a warm-side surface of roughly 88-95 degrees Fahrenheit for most species — about 95 for a bearded dragon's basking zone, 88-90 for a leopard gecko or ball python warm hide — and a cool end in the high 70s so the animal can shuttle.

Skip loose substrate entirely during quarantine. No soil, no bark, no sand. You need to inspect feces daily, and loose substrate hides parasites, mites, and abnormal droppings better than anything else humans have invented. Paper towels let you see stool color, consistency, urates, and any wigglers the moment they appear. Yes, it looks clinical. It's supposed to.

Day One Through Day Seven: Hands Off, Eyes On

The first week is for doing almost nothing. Set the animal up, offer water, and leave it alone. No handling, no introduction to other pets, no photoshoot with the snake draped over your neck. Reptiles process stress slowly, and shipping stress — because even a store-bought animal was likely shipped somewhere along the line — suppresses immune function and appetite for days.

What you DO during week one is observe. I keep a cheap notebook next to every quarantine tub and log four things daily: posture (is it alert, holding its head normally, breathing with a closed mouth?), appetite (did it eat, and if not, is it drinking?), stool (present? formed? normal colored urates?), and behavior (basking normally, exploring at expected times of day, or hiding 24/7?). Open-mouth breathing, wheezing clicks, bubbles at the nostrils, a kinked posture, or stargazing — head tilted upward — all go straight to the vet, not to a Facebook group.

Feed lightly the first week if the animal is a lizard. A hungry insect-eating species can have a modest meal around day three or four. Snakes I typically wait a full week before offering the first meal, and if it refuses, I don't panic and I don't start shoving food at it every other day. One properly sized offer per week is plenty; a stressed snake refusing food is normal for a while.

Week Two Through Week Four: Fecals, Feeding, and the First Real Test

Once the animal has produced a stool — and it will, usually within the first week — bag it and get it to a vet for a fecal exam. A direct smear plus a floatation test runs about $25-60 at most exotic vets and screens for the parasites that cause the most trouble: pinworms, hookworms, coccidia, and flagellates. According to the Association of Reptilian and Amphibian Veterinarians (ARAV), a large percentage of newly acquired reptiles — particularly those from large-scale breeding operations, wholesalers, and expos — carry some parasite load, and many of them show zero symptoms until they're stressed by rehoming. A follow-up fecal three to four weeks later catches parasites that were shedding below detection levels the first time. Two negative fecals is my personal standard before an animal leaves quarantine.

This is also the stretch where hidden problems start announcing themselves. Mites, if present, multiply to visible numbers by weeks two or three — look for tiny black or red specks around the eyes, chin, and vent, or floating in the water bowl. Early respiratory infections often surface once the animal has settled and its energy budget frees up. Appetite either normalizes or doesn't, and a reptile that still refuses appropriate temperatures and proper food after three full weeks gets a vet visit, not more waiting. I've waited out ball python fasts that lasted four months with no ill effect, but that decision came after a clean fecal, a vet exam, and verified husbandry — not as a default.

Handle only as much as needed for health checks during this window. If taming matters to you, short sessions of a few minutes are fine once the animal is eating and eliminating normally, but a hands-off quarantine produces a healthier animal even if it costs you some socialization progress. You can always earn trust in week seven. You can't un-infect a collection.

Week Five Through Day Sixty (or Ninety): The Long Boring Part That Actually Works

The back half of quarantine is uneventful on purpose. You're maintaining the routine: clean paper, fresh water, consistent temps, weekly feeds, daily log entries. This stretch exists because several of the nastiest reptile pathogens have long incubation or low-grade phases. Nidovirus in pythons, for example, can present as nothing more than intermittent regurgitation or a mild wet rasp that comes and goes over weeks. Cryptosporidium in leopard geckos and ball pythons can smolder for months. According to the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA), quarantine duration should always account for species-specific disease incubation periods, and for reptiles that pushes the minimum well past the 30 days many casual keepers use.

My rule: 60 days minimum for lizards, 90 for snakes, and the clock resets if anything abnormal occurs. Regurgitation, a sudden appetite crash, mites, abnormal stool, wheezing — any of those resets quarantine to day one after resolution, because you're no longer watching an unknown, you're watching an illness play out. Animals sourced from expos, imports, or collections you know nothing about get the full 90 regardless of species. Yes, this is annoying. It's also the entire reason it works.

The Hygiene Rules That Make or Break Everything

The enclosure being separate means nothing if your hands aren't. Wash thoroughly with soap and hot water between animals, or better, handle quarantined animals while wearing disposable nitrile gloves and toss them after. Keep disinfectant in the quarantine room — I use a dedicated spray bottle of a veterinary-grade disinfectant plus paper towels that never leave that room. Feed the new animal last, clean its tub last, and if you use feeding tongs or hooks in there, they stay in there. Shoes matter too if the quarantine room shares flooring with your animal room; a cheap pair of slip-on clogs that live by the door is a five-dollar insurance policy against tracking mite eggs around your house.

Bugs from quarantined animals never touch your main colony's feeder supply. If you feed the new arrival from your roach or cricket bin, you've potentially contaminated the bin — and everything you feed from it afterward. Keep a small separate container of feeders for quarantine animals. This one habit has saved me more grief than any other, and I've watched two different keepers nuke thriving Dubia colonies by fishing feeders out with the same dirty cup they used in a quarantine tub.

Common Quarantine Mistakes I See Constantly

Cutting it to two weeks because 'it looks fine' tops the list. Looks mean nothing; that's the entire premise. Second is quarantining in the same room as the collection — airborne transmission matters less for reptiles than for birds, but mites travel, hands wander, and shared equipment happens when everything's within arm's reach. Third is the no-heat bare tub, which is animal neglect dressed up as biosecurity. Fourth is treating every symptom with over-the-counter 'reptile remedies' instead of a fecal and a vet. Store-shelf cures for parasites are mostly useless and sometimes dangerous; fenbendazole and metronidazole dosing needs a vet's scale and species knowledge. And fifth, the sneaky one: buying two new animals from two different sources and quarantining them together. They're not the same risk. If animal A is clean and animal B came from a sketchy expo table, they now both carry animal B's risk profile, and you've learned nothing useful. One animal per quarantine enclosure, always.

Introducing the Graduate: The Last Mile

Day 60 or 90 arrives, the log shows weeks of normal eating, normal stools, two clean fecals, and zero symptoms. Now you move the animal to its permanent enclosure — and here's the part people fumble: disinfect or dispose of everything in the quarantine tub. Paper goes in the trash outside, hides and bowls get scrubbed with disinfectant and rinsed, and the tub itself gets wiped down and stored dry. If the animal had mites at any point, I'd treat the tub with a mite product, let it air for days, and still consider replacing cheap porous items outright. Then, for the first week in the big enclosure, keep logging daily. The move itself is a stressor, and it's your last structured chance to catch a late-developing issue early.

Keep the quarantine tub. Never break it down permanently. The hobby has a way of making sure the day you have no quarantine setup ready is the day you impulse-buy a $400 gecko at a show. My standby tub has handled new arrivals, post-vet recovery, a mite scare in 2019, and one juvenile monitor who needed six weeks of monitored weight gain before joining a big enclosure. It has paid for itself several hundred times over.

The Takeaway

Quarantine is the cheapest veterinary medicine you will ever practice. Sixty to ninety days, a separate room, dedicated tools, a thermostat-guarded heat source, paper substrate, daily notes, and two negative fecals — that's the entire system. No gadget substitutes for it and no seller's reputation exempts you from it, because good breeders get sick animals too and honest ones will tell you quarantine is your job, not theirs. Do the boring part. Your collection's future self will thank you the day a new arrival turns out to be carrying something ugly that never made it past the spare room.
